pages.summary: The Delaunay triangulation of points: triangles (or tetrahedra, or simplices in n dimensions) whose circumcircles hold no other point.
body: Of all triangulations of the points it avoids thin triangles as far as possible. `delaunay` gives a row of point indices for each triangle (tetrahedron in 3-D); `delaunayn` works in any number of dimensions, with Qhull options. `delaunayTriangulation` gives the same as an object to query.

examples.title: Random points triangulated
The simplices of a cube's corners

pages.summary: The convex hull of points: the smallest convex region holding them, and its area or volume.
body: In 2-D, `convhull` gives a closed loop of point indices, counterclockwise, and the area; in 3-D the hull's triangles and the volume. `convhulln` works in any number of dimensions, a row of indices for each facet.

examples.title: A hull round random points
The unit cube's volume
examples.code:
[a, b, c] = ndgrid(0:1);
[~, V] = convhulln([a(:) b(:) c(:)])

pages.summary: The Voronoi diagram of points: the regions of the plane closer to each point than to any other.
body: `voronoi(x, y)` draws its edges (with the points), or with outputs gives the edges' ends to draw. `voronoin` works in any number of dimensions and gives the vertices and, for each point, the indices of its cell's vertices; the first vertex is at infinity, so a cell holding index 1 is unbounded.

examples.title: The diagram of a few points

pages.summary: The simplex enclosing each point, and the nearest point of a set.
body: `tsearchn` finds, for each query point, the triangle (simplex) of a triangulation that holds it (NaN outside) and its barycentric coordinates there. `dsearchn` gives the index of the nearest point of a set, and the distance.
syntax: The enclosing simplex and barycentric coordinates.
The nearest point and its distance.
With `outval` for points outside the hull.

examples.title: In which triangle, and nearest to what

body: Rectangles are rows `[x y width height]`; the result has a row for each rectangle of A and a column for each of B.

pages.summary: Triangles drawn: their edges in the plane, a surface over them, or a mesh.
body: `triplot(T, x, y)` draws the edges of the triangles; `trisurf(T, x, y, z)` fills the triangles as a surface coloured by z (or `c`); `trimesh` draws them as a mesh of coloured edges.
